newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate sets no cut-off for Bosnia troops.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate sets no cut-off for Bosnia troops.

text.p: The U.S. Senate on Friday strongly urged but did not require the United States to pull out its troops from Bosnia by next June 30, giving the White House the flexibility it sought for the peace-keeping mission.
The House has voted to cut off funds for the troops on June 30, 1998, despite the Clinton administration's arguments that a mandatory date could threaten U.S. troops and their mission.
The House and Senate positions will have to be reconciled in a conference.

The nonbinding sense of the Senate amendment, offered by Michigan Democratic Sen. Carl Levin, passed on a voice vote on a bipartisan basis. It was part of a $268 billion defence spending bill which the Senate was wrapping up on Friday.
The Bosnia vote was a compromise that put the Senate firmly on record as seeking an end to U.S. military involvement within a year, but avoiding a confrontation with the administration.
"United States ground combat forces should not participate in a follow-on force in Bosnia and Herzegovina after June 1998," the amendment said.
The Levin measure added that Western European allies should be on notice as of now that they will have to step in with a follow-up force as necessary.

Sen. Russell Feingold, a Wisconsin Democrat, had initially spearheaded an effort for a firmer cut-off date, saying without a deadline the "the mission absolutely risks continuing for who knows how long." But he ended up backing the Levin alternative.

President Bill Clinton also says he wants the troops out next year, but does not want U.S. hands tied in a way that could damage the mission to help create stability in Bosnia within the framework of the Dayton peace pact.
A recent letter from the White House to Congress said a cut-off date could lead to a veto for the whole defence authorisation bill.
"Such an amendment could jeopardise the safety of our troops and damage our national security interests," White House budget director Franklin Raines wrote in that letter last month.

"It would seriously undercut the U.S. commitment to help implement the Dayton Peace Accord and successfully complete the NATO-led misison in Bosnia, resulting in a serious loss in U.S. credibility with the Bosnian parties, with our allies, and with other countries participating in the stabilisation force operation."
Delaware Democrat Sen. Joe Biden, who backed the Levin approach, said some flexibility was necessary for a mission to succeed.
"All we've accomplished in Bosnia would fall apart and what remains to be accomplished would never get off the drawing board," he said.
